source.title: Scaling Experiments in Self-Supervised Cross-Table Representation Learning
source.authors: Maximilian Schambach; D. Paul; J. Otterbach

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some appendix figure text is garbled, but this does not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how downstream linear-probe performance scales in tabular models, a different modality from the language-model setting in the claim.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the reported downstream linear-probe scaling results (Figures 3 and 7 and their accompanying text). The paper also reports training imputation-loss and accuracy curves, but does not report held-out loss or fit and evaluate a power law; those curves therefore do not establish the power-law versions of the claim.
record.test_reason: The study scales tabular Transformers (13k to 16M backbone parameters) trained by masked-cell recovery and reports qualitative linear-probe trends. Every version is about a different construct. V1 to V4 and V6 concern language models. V5 needs the power-law form to hold in a new modality, but the paper fits no power law. It reports only training loss, not held-out loss, and no numbers for downstream trends. Its scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report that linear-probe accuracy generally rises with model scale in both setups. Single-table models saturate early, especially on small datasets. Cross-table pretraining gives only slight improvements, likely limited by too little training data or compute. Longer cross-table pretraining does not systematically improve downstream performance, despite better pretraining imputation accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains tabular Transformers on masked-cell recovery and evaluates linear-probe performance; it does not use the language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Single-table results saturate earlier on smaller datasets; cross-table outcomes vary by dataset and by whether the backbone is frozen or updated during transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: In self-supervised tabular Transformers (13k to 16M parameters), linear-probe performance rises slightly with model size in single-table training. It saturates at the M model on small datasets but not on Cover Type or HIGGS. With cross-table pretraining there is no strong gain with size, and performance worsens on California Housing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream (linear-probe) performance of self-supervised tabular models improves with model scale only when pretraining data is scaled with it.

fits_no_version.finding: In cross-table models, the pretraining training loss falls with tokens processed and imputation accuracy rises. Downstream linear-probe performance does not improve systematically across checkpoints from 250M to 1,500M tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In tabular cross-table pretraining, gains in pretraining objective do not translate into downstream linear-probe gains.

record.problems: The evaluation covers five curated benchmark datasets and reports mostly qualitative scaling trends. The paper states that it does not perform hyperparameter optimization; cross-table training is compute-limited, and its loss curves are training curves rather than held-out loss measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were added for imputation training-loss or imputation-accuracy curves: the paper does not report held-out loss or assess a power-law fit. Exact plotted linear-probe values were not transcribed because the text does not state them.

untested.parts: No language models. Held-out pretraining loss is never measured or fitted.
Depth and width change together across S to XL. Shape is never varied at a fixed parameter count.
Tabular modality, but no power-law form is fitted or checked. Only training-loss curves are shown.
No language-model downstream tasks. The link from pretraining loss to downstream performance is described only qualitatively, for tabular models.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Pretraining training-loss curves against tokens processed. Cross-table: Figure 5, where the XL loss is hardly saturated. Single-table: Figure 6, which shows early saturation and a double-descent-like loss for the L model on HELOC and California Housing. These are training loss only, with no power-law fit.
missing.versions: V5 (cannot_determine: training loss only, no fit)

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6. But V6 belongs to a language-model claim family, and other modalities fall under V5, which requires a power-law form. This paper fits no power law, reports only qualitative trends read from figures, and has no held-out loss. The reader's labels (supports, limits_scope, challenges on V6) are therefore dropped. The model-size sweep also changes several factors at once: training samples differ per model (5M, 10M, 25M) in the single-table setup, and tokenizer parameters (2M to 6M) are large relative to the backbones.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit power laws on small runs or test those fits against much larger runs.
It does not identify or fit compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
It does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The study uses tabular models and self-supervised training, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in this setting.
It tests tabular linear-probe performance against model scale and pretraining duration, not language-model downstream tasks or whether pretraining loss predicts downstream performance.
It does not compare fitting choices or test whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with setup.
